concepts.def: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Nature & Variety of Living Organisms — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Nature & Variety of Living Organisms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Nature & Variety of Living Organisms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: What are the three repeated stages of one PCR cycle?
options: Denaturation (high temp, strands separate), annealing (lower temp, primers bind), extension (Taq polymerase synthesises new strands).
PCR has just one stage — heating the DNA until it copies itself.
PCR uses enzymes from bacteria to cut DNA into fragments, then sticks them back together.
Capillaries split open to release blood and cool the body.

mcqs.q: How do decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere?
options: Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
Capillaries split open to release blood and cool the body.
They respire — breaking down dead organic matter and releasing CO2.
Decomposers release carbon by physically breaking matter into smaller pieces.

mcqs.q: When you are too hot, what happens to the arterioles in your skin?
options: Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
Capillaries split open to release blood and cool the body.
The blood vessels move up to the surface of the skin to release heat.
They vasodilate — more blood flows close to the skin surface, releasing heat to the environment by radiation.

mcqs.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
options: 500 bacteria
400 bacteria
250 bacteria

mcqs.q: An organism has a cell wall made of chitin, feeds by releasing enzymes onto food and absorbing the products, and is not green. It belongs to the:
options: Fungi
Plants
Animals

mcqs.q: A virus can only reproduce inside a host cell. Which statement best describes a virus?
options: It is not a cell and has no cytoplasm or own respiration.
It is a small bacterium with no nucleus.
It is a single-celled animal.
It makes its own food by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which feature do all living organisms share?
options: They respire to release energy.
They photosynthesise.
They have a nervous system.
They have cell walls.

mcqs.q: Pathogens such as Plasmodium (which causes malaria) are single-celled eukaryotes. They are classified as:
